title: Backup storage accounts
description: On AWS, management can make each server’s backup storage key itself and revoke it when the server is revoked, so no key outlives its server and none is copied by hand. Add a storage account once for each AWS account, then choose it when you add an S3 backup destination.
loadFailed: Storage accounts could not be loaded.
empty: No storage accounts yet. Backup destinations use storage keys you make and limit yourself.

account.path: IAM path of the users management makes
account.rotationEvery_one: Management replaces each destination’s key when it is {{count}} day old.
account.rotationEvery_other: Management replaces each destination’s key when it is {{count}} days old.
account.rotationOff: Off. Keys stay in use until you rotate them.
account.extraKeys_one: The latest check found {{count}} access key that management didn’t make on one of its users, and deleted it. Someone holding the admin key may have made it.
account.extraKeys_other: The latest check found {{count}} access keys that management didn’t make on its users, and deleted them. Someone holding the admin key may have made them.
account.peersDescription: Users these installations make in this AWS account are shown as theirs. Each with the permissions boundary raises an alert until you acknowledge it, since someone holding the admin key can make a user with a peer’s tag.

found.title: Users management didn’t make
found.description: The latest check found these IAM users under this workspace’s path with no record here. One may have been restored from an older management backup, made by another installation, or made with a leaked admin key.
found.peer: Tagged by a peer installation, and acknowledged on {{date}}.
found.peerUnacknowledged: Tagged by a peer installation, and no acknowledgement covers it as the latest check found it. Someone holding the admin key can make a user with a peer’s tag, or give another access key to one you acknowledged, so it raises an alert until you acknowledge it. If that installation didn’t make it, revoke it and replace the admin key.
found.peerUnrecorded: Tagged by a peer installation. The next successful check records what you’d acknowledge.
found.acknowledgeDescription: Acknowledge it only if that installation made it, for example a server this workspace was transferred to. Management then shows it without an alert, and never revokes it. This covers IAM user ID {{id}} with access keys {{keys}}: a user made again under this name, or given another access key, raises the alert again.
found.acknowledgeDescriptionNoKeys: Acknowledge it only if that installation made it, for example a server this workspace was transferred to. Management then shows it without an alert, and never revokes it. This covers IAM user ID {{id}}, which has no access keys: a user made again under this name, or given an access key, raises the alert again.
found.unbounded: It has no permissions boundary, so the admin key can’t revoke it. Delete it in the AWS console.
found.revokeFailing: Management is revoking it, and its last attempt failed: {{reason}}
found.revokeDescription: Management takes away the user’s access and deletes it at AWS. Anything using its key, such as another installation’s backups, stops working. This can’t be undone. If nobody you know made it, replace the admin key too, since whoever made it may hold it.
found.revokePeerDescription: It’s tagged by peer installation {{installation}}, and no acknowledgement covers it as the latest check found it. If that installation made it, a server this workspace was transferred to or from may still use its key, and that server’s backups would fail. Revoke it only if you don’t recognise it, and then replace the admin key, since whoever made it may hold it. Management takes away the user’s access and deletes it at AWS. This can’t be undone.
found.addPeerDescription: Users it makes in this AWS account are then shown as its. Each with the permissions boundary raises an alert until you acknowledge it by name, and once acknowledged, management never revokes it. Add only an installation this workspace was transferred to or from.

add.instructions: Create the permissions boundary policy first. Then give an IAM user outside /astilba/ a policy that lets it manage only users under {{path}} that carry the boundary, and enter its access key here. Management checks the key with AWS before storing it and never shows it again.
add.label: Add storage account
add.name: Account name

replace.instructions: The new key must belong to the same AWS account. Keys management already made keep working. Delete the old admin key at AWS afterwards.
replace.boundaryStays: The account keeps this permissions boundary, since every user management made under it carries it. To use another boundary, add another storage account.
replace.label: Replace the admin key of {{name}}
replace.replaced: Admin key replaced. Delete the old one at AWS.

rotation.description: Management replaces each destination’s key when it reaches this age, without revoking its server. The old key is revoked once the server installs the new one. 90 days follows the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark.
rotation.days: Maximum key age in days, from 30 to 365
rotation.offDescription: Each key stays in use until you rotate it, so a leaked key keeps working until then.
rotation.label: Key rotation of {{name}}

destinations.title: Destinations using this account
destinations.none: No destination uses this account yet. Choose it when you add an S3 backup destination.

destination.exposed: A revoked server may still hold one of this destination’s keys, so it could delete or overwrite these backups. Management revokes its keys itself; this ends an hour after AWS confirms them revoked.
destination.remintFailed: Management couldn’t make a new key for this destination and keeps trying: {{reason}}
destination.rotationRequested: A new key has been asked for. Management is making it.
destination.rotating: Management is replacing this destination’s key. The old key is revoked once {{server}} installs the new one, so a server that is offline keeps using it until then.
destination.rotationOverdue: The key was due to be replaced on {{date}}. Management is replacing it.
destination.rotateDescription: Management makes {{server}} a new key and installs it on the destination’s backup policies. The old key keeps working until the server reports the new one, and management then revokes it, so backups carry on. If the key has leaked, revoke it instead: that stops it at once, but backups can fail until the server installs its new key.

key.label: {{purpose}} for {{server}}
key.handedOver: Handed over to a workspace transfer
key.failing_one: Revoking it has failed {{count}} time: {{reason}} Fix the cause, then retry.
key.failing_other: Revoking it has failed {{count}} times: {{reason}} Fix the cause, then retry.
key.revokeCurrent: Management revokes the key at AWS, and makes the server a new one if it has no other key in use. The server’s backups can fail until it has installed a key that isn’t revoked, such as one from a rotation under way.
key.revokeHandedOver: This key was handed over to a workspace transfer. Revoking it breaks the transferred server’s backups, which can then no longer reach this bucket.
key.revokeRecovery: The restore using it can no longer read its snapshot. Management revokes it itself once the restore ends.

failure.credentialRefused: AWS no longer accepts the account’s admin key. Replace it.
failure.accessDenied: AWS refused the request. Check that the admin policy is still attached to the admin user.
failure.notFound: AWS couldn’t find the user or key.
failure.notAdmin: The admin key no longer belongs to an IAM user outside /astilba/.
failure.accountChanged: The admin key now belongs to another AWS account. Replace it with a key of the account it was added with.
failure.unavailable: AWS couldn’t be reached or failed.
failure.userMissing: Its IAM user is gone at AWS.
failure.deleteConflict: AWS won’t delete the user while something else is attached to it, such as a console password, an MFA device, a group or another policy. Management keeps it denied all access meanwhile. Remove those in the AWS console so management can delete it.
failure.notListed: AWS refused the request for the user, and doesn’t list it under the workspace’s path, which is how IAM can answer for a user that no longer exists. Management counts it revoked once the user, if it existed, would be listed.
failure.movedOffPath: The user is no longer under the workspace’s path, so the admin key can’t change it, but AWS still accepts its key. Someone with wider IAM rights moved it. Delete the user in the AWS console, or move it back so management can revoke it.
